cards.h: A question with no easy answer
cards.b:
A rock, a flame and a seed all look quiet from far away. Yet only one of them is alive. Biology starts with a simple question: what makes the seed different?

There is no single test. Scientists instead list a set of traits that living things share. Knowing the list helps you read every later lesson, from cells to ecosystems.

Most textbooks use a checklist. A living thing:

  • Is made of cells (one or many).
  • Uses energy to run its chemistry.
  • Grows and develops.
  • Reproduces.
  • Responds to its surroundings.
  • Keeps a stable inside (homeostasis).
  • Evolves over generations.

Think of it like a shop: it needs stock (matter), power (energy), a counter that reacts to customers, and branches that open over time.

Your body stays near 37 °C whether it is Delhi in June or Shimla in January. This is homeostasis, coined by Walter Cannon in 1926 building on Claude Bernard's idea of a steady inner environment.

  1. A sensor notices a change (you get hot).
  2. A control centre compares it with a set point.
  3. An effector acts (you sweat).
  4. The change shrinks and the loop stops.

It works like a room thermostat.

Metabolism is all the chemical reactions in a cell. Some build things (anabolic), like making protein. Some break things down (catabolic), like burning glucose for energy.

A fire also uses fuel and gives off heat, but a fire does not regulate itself, grow by its own plan or pass on instructions. Life does all three.

Life is built in layers, each with new abilities.

A single bacterium is one cell and one organism. You are about 30 trillion cells working together.

In 1665 Robert Hooke saw tiny boxes in cork and called them cells. Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) said all living things are made of cells. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that every cell comes from a pre-existing cell.

Together these form the cell theory.

A virus has genes and evolves, but it has no cell and cannot make energy. It reproduces only inside a host cell. Many biologists call it non-living outside a host; others call it a 'life-like' agent. It shows that the line is fuzzy.

People once believed maggots arose from rotting meat. In 1668 Francesco Redi covered some jars with gauze and found no maggots on the meat. In 1859 Louis Pasteur used swan-neck flasks: broth stayed clear because germs could not reach it. This ended the idea of spontaneous generation.

In 1953 Stanley Miller sparked gases like early Earth's and made amino acids, showing how life's building blocks may have formed.

Check yourself

  • Moving does not equal alive. Clouds and rivers move; plants barely do.
  • Growth is not just getting bigger. Crystals grow, but from outside, not by metabolism.
  • A mule is alive even though it cannot reproduce. Traits are judged for the whole group of life, not each individual.

cards.h: J.C. Bose and the response of plants
cards.b: Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858-1937) built the crescograph, which magnified plant growth by about ten thousand times or more. He showed that plants respond to touch, heat and chemicals in measurable ways, blurring the line between 'living' responses in plants and animals. He founded the Bose Institute in Kolkata in 1917.

• Life is defined by a checklist: cells, energy, growth, reproduction, response, homeostasis, evolution.
  • Cell theory: all life is cellular and cells come from cells.
  • Redi and Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation.
  • Viruses sit on the edge of the definition.

Think about it:

  1. Why is fire not alive though it uses fuel and grows?
  2. Would you call a virus alive? Defend your view.

o: It grows by adding material outside, without metabolism
